extracted.intended_audience: undergraduate or beginning graduate students in real analysis / mathematics needing linear algebra, polynomial, and set-theory background
extracted.subtask_description: Concise background material covering linear algebra (matrices, determinants, rank), polynomial factorization and roots, and basic set theory (partial orders, Zorn's Lemma, cardinality) used as tools in real analysis. Includes definitions, key theorems, and computational facts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dot product on F^m (real/complex column vectors)
rubrics_metrics.description: Define a dot product in F^m by (a1,...,am) · (b1,...,bm) = a1 b1 + ··· + am bm with no complex conjugations involved.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Used to give a tidy correspondence between linear functions and matrices in the standard bases; choice here is the real/field dot product (no conjugation) so one must be careful when relating to Hermitian inner products.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correspondence between linear maps and matrices
rubrics_metrics.description: A linear function T in L(F^n, F^m) corresponds to an m-by-n matrix A with entries in F via Ai j = T(ej) · ui.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Under this correspondence kernel(T) corresponds to null space of A, image(T) corresponds to column space of A; composition of linear maps corresponds to matrix multiplication in the same written order.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rank and dimension relations (rank-nullity)
rubrics_metrics.description: dim(domain of T) = dim(kernel of T) + dim(image of T). The rank of A (or T) is dim(span of columns of A) = dim(span of rows of A).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Row reduction shows dim(null space of A) + dim(span of rows of A) = number of columns; argument with bases shows the rank-nullity identity. Use these equalities to compute rank and relate row/column spaces.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determinant characterization (three defining properties)
rubrics_metrics.description: The determinant function det on square matrices over F is uniquely defined by: (i) det A is linear in each row when other rows are fixed; (ii) det A = 0 if two rows are equal; (iii) det I = 1 for the identity matrix.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These properties allow computation of det A via row reduction: row replacement leaves determinant unchanged, scaling a row multiplies determinant by scalar, and row interchange multiplies determinant by -1. After reduction either RREF = I implies det=1 or a zero row implies det=0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Additional determinant consequences and identities
rubrics_metrics.description: Consequences listed include: det A = 0 iff A is invertible; det(A^tr) = det A; det(AB) = (det A)(det B); explicit permutation formula and cofactor expansion; Cramer's rule when det A ≠ 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permutation formula: det A = sum_{σ} (sgn σ) Π_i A_{i,σ(i)}. Expansion by cofactors and Cramer's rule give explicit solution entries x_j = det(A_j)/det(A) where A_j replaces j-th column by b. Use these identities for proofs and computations; they follow from the defining properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Division Algorithm for polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: If A(X) and B(X) are polynomials over F with B(X) ≠ 0, then there exist unique polynomials Q(X) and R(X) with A = B Q + R and either R = 0 or deg R < deg B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This codifies polynomial long division; proof by induction on deg A. Uniqueness is via contradiction using degree bounds. Use to compute quotients and remainders and to deduce the Factor Theorem.

rubrics_metrics.name: Factor Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: For r in F and polynomial P, (X − r) divides P iff P(r) = 0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Direct consequence of Division Algorithm: write P = (X − r)Q + R with deg R < 1, evaluate at r to deduce R = P(r). Useful for factoring polynomials once roots are found.

rubrics_metrics.name: Roots bound proposition
rubrics_metrics.description: A nonzero polynomial P of degree n over F has at most n distinct roots.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prove by induction using the Factor Theorem: if r1,...,rk distinct roots then (X−r1)···(X−rk) divides P, leading to degree comparison.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition of greatest common divisor and Euclidean algorithm for polynomials
rubrics_metrics.description: Given polynomials A and B (B ≠ 0), the Euclidean algorithm produces remainders R1,...,Rn with decreasing degrees; Rn (nonzero) is a greatest common divisor (gcd) of A and B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Properties: gcd is unique up to scalar multiplication; any common divisor divides the gcd; there exist polynomials P and Q with A P + B Q = D where D is gcd (Bezout identity). Use division steps A = B Q1 + R1, etc., until remainder 0.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma: prime polynomial divisibility
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is a prime (irreducible) polynomial and P divides AB then P divides A or P divides B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses gcd: if P doesn't divide A, gcd(A,P) = 1 so there exist S,T with AS + PT = 1; multiply by B and use divisibility to conclude P divides B. This is the analogue of Euclid's lemma for polynomials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique factorization of polynomials over F
rubrics_metrics.description: Every nonzero polynomial of degree ≥ 1 over F is a product of prime (irreducible) polynomials. Factorization is unique up to order and scalar multiples of factors.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Existence by induction on degree (factor non-prime factors into lower-degree factors until prime). Uniqueness uses the lemma that a prime dividing a product divides one factor and cancellation after adjusting leading coefficients to 1.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fundamental Theorem of Algebra (statement)
rubrics_metrics.description: Any polynomial with complex coefficients and degree ≥ 1 has at least one root in C.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consequences: over C, every prime polynomial has degree 1, hence every nonzero polynomial factors as c Π (X − z_l). Proofs can use complex analysis (Liouville), topology (Heine–Borel), or algebra (Galois theory) in different contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiplicity and factorization over C
rubrics_metrics.description: If P is nonzero of degree n over C with roots r1,...,rk then P(X) = c Π_j (X − r_j)^{m_j} with unique positive integers m_j summing to n (multiplicities).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Group like linear factors from unique factorization; multiplicities counted by power of (X − r_j). Useful for root counting and analytic arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definitions and properties of partial orderings, chains, and maximal elements
rubrics_metrics.description: A partial ordering ≤ on S is reflexive and transitive. A chain is a totally ordered subset. An upper bound for a chain T is an element u with c ≤ u for all c in T. A maximal element m satisfies that no strictly larger element exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish partial ordering from total (linear) ordering (additional comparability property). These notions are prerequisites to Zorn's Lemma and well-ordering arguments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zorn's Lemma (statement and basic use)
rubrics_metrics.description: If S is a nonempty partially ordered set in which every chain has an upper bound, then S has a maximal element.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Commonly used with Axiom of Choice; example application: existence of a basis of any real vector space by considering the family of linearly independent subsets ordered by inclusion and applying Zorn's Lemma to get a maximal independent set which spans.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lemma used in Zorn proof (fixed-point-like admissible set lemma)
rubrics_metrics.description: If X is a nonempty partially ordered set in which every chain has a least upper bound and f: X → X satisfies x ≤ f(x) for all x, then there exists x0 with f(x0) = x0.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical lemma used in the proof of Zorn's Lemma to construct admissible sets and obtain a fixed point (maximal chain). The proof builds minimal admissible sets and shows they are chains closed under f.

rubrics_metrics.name: Zermelo's Well-ordering Theorem (corollary)
rubrics_metrics.description: Every set has a well-ordering.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Applied by forming certain chains of well-ordered initial segments and invoking Zorn's Lemma to obtain a maximal well-ordered subset which must equal the whole set.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cardinality: Schroeder–Bernstein Theorem
rubrics_metrics.description: If there exist one-to-one maps f: A → B and g: B → A then A and B have the same cardinality (there exists a bijection).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Constructive proof via partitioning A and B into invariant subsets under compositions of f and g and defining a bijection piecewise; the text gives an explicit decomposition into disjoint unions A = ⋃ An ∪ ⋃ A0n etc.

rubrics_metrics.name: Comparability of cardinals via Zorn's Lemma
rubrics_metrics.description: For any two sets A and B, either there is a one-to-one function from A into B or one from B into A (i.e., their cardinalities are comparable in the ≤ sense).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof uses Zorn's Lemma on the family of one-one partial maps ordered by inclusion to obtain a maximal injection whose domain or image must be whole set, yielding an injection in one direction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cantor's theorem (power set has larger cardinality)
rubrics_metrics.description: For any set A, the power set 2^A has strictly larger cardinality than A.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diagonal argument: any purported map F: A → 2^A misses the subset E = {x ∈ A : x ∉ F(x)}, so F is not onto. Also shows existence of uncountable sets starting from any set A.
